Name: PLC Overview
Description: A brief overview of how PLC's work
Author: mgriffis

ContentBlocks.TextContent:
What does PLC stand for?
A) Programmable Latch Controller
*B) Programmable Logic Controller
C) Process Logic Controller

What industry did PLC's first appear in?
A) Aerospace 
B) Mining
*C) Automotive
D) Tire Manufacturing

What are the main hardware componets of a PLC?
*A) CPU, power supply, memory, I/O, communicaitons processor
B) CPU, power supply, analog sensors, I/O
C) CPU, memory, I/O, input card

What is order of a basic PLC scan cycle?
A) Outputs, program processing, inputs
B) Inputes, outputs, program processing
*C) Inputs, program processing, outputs

What kind of sensor are the load cells for upset force on a MPAC?
A) Digital
*B) Analog
C) Thermocouple
D) RTD probe

ContentBlocks.PlainTextContent:
How a Drive Creates AC Power from DC:

Most industrial drive modules (VFDs / servo drives) do not receive AC power directly from the PLC. Instead, they create their own AC waveform internally, even though the incoming power is DC (or converted to DC first).

Step 1 — AC Is Converted to DC (The DC Bus)
Even if a drive is powered by AC:
-The drive rectifies AC into DC

This DC is stored on a DC bus using capacitors

Why?
-DC is easier to control precisely
-It provides a stable energy source

Think of the DC bus as a “battery inside the drive.”

Step 2 — Switching Devices Chop the DC
Inside the drive are high-speed electronic switches:
-IGBTs or MOSFETs
-These switch thousands of times per second
-They rapidly turn DC on and off in controlled patterns.

Step 3 — Pulse Width Modulation (PWM)
The drive uses Pulse Width Modulation (PWM):
-DC is sent as pulses
-Pulse width changes over time
-The average voltage rises and falls in a smooth pattern

Although the output is technically a square wave, the motor inductance smooths it into something that behaves like AC.
The motor “sees” a sine wave, even though it’s being fed pulses.

Step 4 — Three-Phase AC Is Recreated
For a three-phase motor, the drive creates:
-Phase U
-Phase V
-Phase W
Each phase:
-Is shifted 120° apart
-Has controlled amplitude and frequency
-This rotating magnetic field is what causes the motor to turn.

Step 5 — Speed & Torque Control
By adjusting:
-Frequency → controls speed
-Voltage / current → controls torque
The drive can:
-Ramp smoothly
-Hold position
-React instantly to load changes

This is why drives outperform direct AC motor starters.
Why This Matters for Troubleshooting

Key takeaway for techs:
If the DC bus is healthy but the motor doesn’t move, the problem is usually control logic, enable signals, or output stages — not incoming power.

Common failures:
-DC bus OK, no output → drive disabled or faulted
-One phase missing → blown output transistor
-Motor hums → incorrect parameters or load issue

Multiplexing & Demultiplexing:
"How Many Signals Share One Cable"


Multiplexing means:
Taking many independent signals and sending them one at a time, very fast, over a single communication path.

Demultiplexing means:
Receiving that combined data stream and sorting each signal back to where it belongs.

This is why:
-Hundreds of I/O points
-Motion data
-Diagnostics
-Safety status

…can all travel over one Ethernet or PROFIBUS cable.

Simple Mental Model:
Think of a mail truck 🚚:
-One truck (cable)
-Many letters (signals)

Each letter has an address (device + data ID)

The truck doesn’t care what the letters are — it just delivers them fast.
Each house (device) opens only the mail addressed to it.

That’s multiplexing in real life.

What Is Being Multiplexed?
On industrial networks, the cable carries:
-Input states
-Output commands
-Encoder values
-Drive feedback
-Diagnostics
-Safety telegrams
All mixed together — but tagged.

How the Tagging Works (Conceptually)
Each chunk of data includes:
-Source (who sent it)
-Destination (who it’s for)
-Type (I/O, motion, safety, diagnostic)
-Order / timing

This allows the receiver to:
-Pull out only its data
-Ignore everything else
-That sorting process is demultiplexing.

Applying This to Real Systems:
-PROFIBUS
-Serial, cyclic communication
-PLC is the master
-Devices respond in assigned order
-Time-sliced multiplexing

Think:
“You talk now. You talk next.”
-PROFINET / Ethernet
-Packet-based
-Data sent in frames
-Multiple conversations interleaved

Think:
“Everyone talks, but packets are labeled.”
Real-time PROFINET just makes sure important packets cut in line.

Why This Replaced Hardwired I/O:
Old way:
-One wire per signal
-Huge cabinets
-Massive troubleshooting effort

Multiplexed networks:
-One cable
-Distributed I/O
-Easier expansion
-Faster diagnostics

This is why remote I/O racks exist at all.

Why Multiplexing Matters for Troubleshooting:
-If the cable fails, everything fails.

Because:
-All signals share the same path

Common symptoms:
-Multiple devices offline at once
-Whole I/O rack disappears
-Drives fault simultaneously

This usually points to:
-Cable
-Connector
-Network device
-Power to remote station
-Not logic.
